  RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         §               BEFORE THE
  LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
  STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                  §                OF TEXAS

LOWER COLORADO RIVER AUTHORITY AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES
   CORPORATION’S COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

       Lower Colorado River Authority and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation

(collectively LCRA) submit these comments and executive summary in response to Commission

Staff’s Proposal for Publication of new 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.194 (PFP), relating to

Large Load Interconnection Standards.


                                  I.     INTRODUCTION

       LCRA introduces several recommendations and redlines to the PFP for the Commission’s

consideration. Most concerning to LCRA is the direct assignment of system upgrade costs to large

load customers. While this is undoubtedly an important policy consideration, cost assignment is

best handled in the Commission’s rulemaking on Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery

(Project No. 58484) through a minimum demand charge allocated to large load customers. As a

related but separate concern, LCRA urges the Commission to streamline the financial security

requirements in manner that supports economic development in Texas while upholding current and

longstanding risk mitigation practices implemented by Transmission Service Providers (TSPs) to

support both customers and the reliability of the transmission grid. Additional recommendations

are provided in the sections that follow, and LCRA appreciates the Commission’s thoughtful

review of these comments.




LCRA AND LCRA TSC COMMENTS                                                         Page 2 of 37
                II.    GENERAL COMMENTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

       16 TAC § 25.194(d) and 16 TAC § 25.194(f) – Three-party agreements
       In the scenario where the interconnecting Distribution Service Provider (DSP) and

interconnecting TSP are different entities, the PFP appropriately recognizes the need for

agreements with the interconnecting large load customer to clearly identify each entity’s

responsibilities. It is important to note that the interconnecting TSP bears a disproportionate share

of the financial and regulatory risk for these types of agreements given its scope during the

interconnection process. As such, it stands to reason that the form for such agreements should be

provided by the interconnecting TSP.

       If the Commission moves towards creating a standard form for such agreements, the

interconnecting TSP must retain the study fee defined in 16 TAC § 25.194(d)(9) for the

performance of any screening and facilities studies, as well as the processing of models and data

requests from ERCOT. Additionally, the interconnecting TSP must hold the financial security as

defined in 16 TAC § 25.194(d)(10) as it holds the greatest amount of financial risk in constructing

the necessary interconnection facilities. At a minimum, a standard form should include the

following:

       1) Term and termination,

       2) Responsibilities for the provision of transmission and retail services,

       3) Load commissioning plan and peak demand,

       4) Financial security requirements and release schedule,

       5) Description of the interconnection facilities,

       6) Project schedule,

       7) Property right and permitting requirements, and

       8) Load operational and system protection requirements.

LCRA AND LCRA TSC COMMENTS                                                             Page 3 of 37
        16 TAC § 25.194(d) – Effective date
       LCRA recommends redlines to the referenced subsection to recognize agreements signed

with large load customers that were in effect ahead of the 2026 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP)

compliance plan date of April 1, 2026. Projects reported by LCRA in this category are in advanced

stages of development and should not be subject to any activities that reset progress.

       16 TAC § 25.194(d)(7) – Power supply
       LCRA recommends redlines to the referenced subsections and paragraph to require

additional details to highlight whether on-site generation is in front of or behind the meter. From

an interconnecting TSP perspective, this is an important detail to provide as it will have system

planning and reliability implications.

       16 TAC § 25.194(d)(9), (d)(11)(A), and (d)(11)(B) – Study fee refundability
       LCRA recommends redlines to the referenced subsections and paragraphs to require

refundability of any unused study fee funds. Requiring the interconnecting TSP to keep track of

and apply unused study fee funds towards significant equipment or services would be an

administratively burdensome task, with no apparent benefit for any party. A more streamlined

approach at this stage would allow for the application of financial security towards significant

equipment and services. Additional redlines introduced by LCRA in 16 TAC § 25.194(d)(11)(A)

will allow for additional financial security to be requested through an amended intermediate

agreement should the amount required under 16 TAC § 25.194(d)(10) be deemed insufficient.

Finally, language was added to reflect that the interconnecting DSP and interconnecting TSP that

are party to the agreement with the large load customer each have separate and distinct costs for

the project. If required and necessary, both entities should be able to amend the intermediate

agreement to request posting of additional financial security for significant equipment or services

under 16 TAC § 25.194(d)(11)(A).


LCRA AND LCRA TSC COMMENTS                                                               Page 4 of 37
        16 TAC § 25.194(d)(10) – Due date for financial security
       LCRA recommends redlines to the referenced subsection and paragraph to allow financial

security to be posted within five business days of executing the intermediate agreement.

Recognizing that the financial security required in this subsection is significant, processing time

may be necessary for large load customers that need to work with financial institutions to fulfill

this requirement.

       16 TAC § 25.194(f) – Grandfathering and appropriate timelines
       LCRA recommends redlines to the referenced subsection to recognize agreements signed

with large load customers that were in effect ahead of the 2026 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP)

compliance plan reporting date of April 1, 2026. Projects reported by LCRA in this category are

in an advanced stage and should not be subject to any activities that reset progress. Additionally,

sixty days is a more reasonable timeline for large load customers to fulfill duties under this

subsection. The posting of significant financial security and CIAC may require a processing time

that is longer than thirty days, and it is best to allow additional flexibility to comply with this

requirement. LCRA also supports changes to conform the timeline for an interconnecting entity’s

notice to ERCOT about a project cancellation to aforementioned redlines in regard to the execution

deadline. Since LCRA increased the execution deadline to sixty days, the notice of cancellation

deadline has also been increased by sixty days (i.e., thirty days after the execution deadline is

missed, the interconnecting entity must give notice to ERCOT).

       16 TAC § 25.194(f)(2) – Substantially similar request
       LCRA recommends redlines to remove this subsection and paragraph. The substantially

similar request disclosure requirement was incorporated at the intermediate agreement stage to

reduce speculative and duplicative requests that lead to inaccurate load forecasting. The inclusion




LCRA AND LCRA TSC COMMENTS                                                            Page 5 of 37
 of this requirement at the intermediate agreement stage accomplishes that goal. When a project

reaches the interconnection agreement stage, this disclosure requirement is unnecessary.

        16 TAC § 25.194(f)(7), (f)(8) and (f)(9) – Interconnection fee, CIAC flexibility, and
        financial security
        LCRA recommends redlines to the referenced subsection and paragraphs to better align

16 TAC § 25.194 with standard risk management practices for transmission project development.

Stated simply, LCRA only requires financial security in amounts necessary to cover the estimated

costs for design, procurement of significant equipment, direct interconnection, and construction

services for any project it undertakes. If a large load customer’s project is cancelled or withdrawn,

LCRA would seek to apply the financial security for the project to any outstanding amounts owed

and then, importantly, refund the remainder to the large load customer. In this frame of reference,

if the dollar per MW financial security amount at the intermediate agreement stage is found to be

insufficient at the interconnection agreement stage, the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting

TSP should be allowed to request additional financial security to cover its expected risk. There is

no need to introduce an additional non-refundable interconnection fee in 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(7).

        Additionally, as mentioned throughout previous verbal and written comments on this

project, LCRA’s current business practice would only require non-refundable CIAC in situations

where requests are made by interconnecting customers that go above and beyond our standard

interconnection practices (e.g., requests to underground transmission lines). TSPs should have the

authority to retain this flexibility.

        Finally, LCRA understands the non-refundable interconnection fee and securitization

approach within the PFP are meant to dually offset costs for interconnection that could potentially

be uplifted to ratepayers and to provide a strong incentive for large load customers to submit

thoughtful and deliberate interconnection requests. We believe these goals can fundamentally be


LCRA AND LCRA TSC COMMENTS                                                             Page 6 of 37
 achieved with the dollar per MW security amount and study fee in the intermediate agreement

stage, along with a minimum demand charge for large load customers (discussed in more detail

below).

         Recommended 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(6) and (f)(7) – Power Supply and Controllable load
         LCRA recommends redlines to incorporate two new paragraphs into the interconnection

agreement stage to provide symmetry to the disclosures required at the intermediate agreement

stage. As an interconnecting TSP, it is important for LCRA to understand whether there have been

any updates to a large load customer’s power procurement plan or controllable load resource

modeling plan since the intermediate agreement stage. Changes to either plan will have system

planning and reliability implications and are necessary to disclose at the interconnection agreement

stage.

         16 TAC § 25.194(f)(10) – System Upgrades
         In the context of the interconnection of large load customers, PURA § 37.0561(b) and

Section 6 of Senate Bill (SB) 6 are meant to work in tandem to minimize the potential for stranded

infrastructure costs and appropriately assign the cost of transmission investment to those that

introduce the need for that investment. With these principles in mind, it is understandable why the

approach in 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(10) was proposed to have each large load customer securitize the

system upgrades necessary for reliable service. However, attributing security requirements for

system upgrades to individual large load customers would be an administratively complex, if not

impossible, exercise to undertake. It is worth noting that when a single component of the

transmission system is upgraded, the benefit is felt in aggregate. For example, if interconnecting a

large load customer at a certain location requires upgrading the voltage level of a nearby

transmission line, the large load customer isn’t the only entity that will benefit from that upgrade.

The increased voltage of the line has the potential to reduce congestion costs borne by all load in


LCRA AND LCRA TSC COMMENTS                                                             Page 7 of 37
 both the immediate area and beyond. The capacity increase on the transmission system may also

allow for other loads (both Large and small) as well as generators to safely interconnect at varying

points (both temporally and locationally) in the future. In that sense, it would be fundamentally

unfair to require a single large load customer to securitize the costs of the entire line upgrade, and

practically impossible to securitize costs from the large load customer based on its exact proportion

of benefit received from the line upgrade as that proportion will naturally decrease over time. For

these reasons, LCRA recommends the removal of 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(10) in the PFP.

       The question of who should pay for the necessary upgrades is best determined in Project

No. 58484. As LCRA has commented in that project, the Commission should evaluate the use of

a minimum demand charge for large load customers based on contracted load ramps produced by

the batch study framework and agreed to by the large load customer during the interconnection

agreement stage. In this way, all beneficiaries of system upgrades will be required to share in the

recovery of costs, and large load customers will contribute to cost recovery proportional to their

maximum reservations on the system. Furthermore, if the Commission ultimately decides to adopt

a minimum demand charge, LCRA recommends adding a requirement in the interconnection

agreement stage where the large load customer agrees to pay a minimum demand charge for a set

period of time (duration determined by Commission). This requirement would ensure that large

load customers are bringing forward thoughtful projects into the interconnection process, as their

minimum demand charge would be a function of their requested load ramp.

       16 TAC § 25.194(g) and 16 TAC § 25.194(h) – Refund of security in event of
       withdrawal or non-utilized capacity
       LCRA proposes redlines to the referenced subsections to reflect a full refund of financial

security in the event of a withdrawal or non-utilized capacity scenario after outstanding amounts

owed are covered. LCRA envisions the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP electing to


LCRA AND LCRA TSC COMMENTS                                                              Page 8 of 37
 either issue an invoice or draw down on the large load customer’s financial security in order to

cover outstanding amounts owed. In the instance that the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting

TSP elects to issue an invoice, and the invoice is not paid within ten business days, the DSP or

TSP must draw down on the large load customer’s financial security for the amounts covered by

the unpaid invoice. Additionally, CIAC should be considered non-refundable for construction costs

incurred. LCRA proposes additional redlines to specify that any remaining balance must be

refunded to the large load customer within 60 days of a project withdrawal or non-utilized capacity

scenario.

       Recommended 16 TAC § 25.194(i)(2) – Waiting period to refund security
       LCRA proposes redlines to the remove the referenced subsection and paragraph. LCRA

agrees with the approach defined in 16 TAC § 25.194(i)(1) whereby 20% of the remaining balance

upon energization is refunded but modifies the language to make it clear that the remainder of

balance is refunded ratably as the large load customer achieves milestones in its schedule for

phased energization.

       Minor changes throughout
       LCRA recommends the phrase “if applicable” throughout the PFP language. This addition

is meant to better inform the reader that the “or” in “interconnecting DSP or, the interconnecting

TSP” is not interchangeable on a whim. The determination of the correct entity for the

corresponding requirement needs to be clearly notated in each agreement that is executed between

an interconnecting DSP, interconnecting TSP, and large load customer, and the use of this phrase

is intended to strengthen that need.

                         III.    PROPOSED REDLINES TO §25.194

§25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.
(a)   Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility,

      a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative to interconnect a large load customer

      to the ERCOT system. Nothing in this section limits the authority of a municipally owned

      utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load

      customers on their systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section.

(b)   Applicability. This section applies to a large load customer that seeks:

      (1)    a new interconnection that is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts (MW);

      (2)    an expanded interconnection that equals or exceeds 75 MW for the first time; and

      (3)    an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.

(c)   Definitions. The following words and terms, when used in this section, have the following

      meanings unless the context indicates otherwise:

      (1)    Backup generating facilities -- Generation facilities or energy storage facilities

             that are not capable of operating, or are not configured to operate, in parallel with

             the ERCOT system and cannot export energy to the ERCOT system.

      (2)    Competitively sensitive information -- Competitively sensitive information

             includes exact site locations, such as parcel identifiers or property boundaries;

             commercial terms, such as pricing or internal development prioritization;

             proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-deployment strategies; and

             financing structures. Competitively sensitive information does not include the

             identity of a large load customer; general site location, such as load zone; requested

             or contracted peak demand; timing of energization; or whether an interconnection

             request is associated with the same applicant or affiliated entities.

LCRA AND LCRA TSC COMMENTS                                                           Page 10 of 37
     (3)   Contracted peak demand -- The total non-coincident peak demand that a large

          load customer requests that an interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP serve

          at a site as stated interconnection agreement.

    (4)   Interconnecting distribution service provider (DSP) -- The electric utility,

          municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that is certificated to provide

          retail electric delivery service at the location in which the large load customer seeks

          to interconnect.

    (5)   Interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP) -- The electric utility,

          municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that owns and operates the

          facilities necessary to interconnect the large load customer to the ERCOT system.

    (6)   Interconnection agreement -- An agreement that is executed by a large load

          customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different from the interconnecting DSP,

          the interconnecting TSP after completion of the interconnection study and that, at a

          minimum, satisfies subsection (f) of this section.

    (7)   Interconnection study -- The set of studies that are required by ERCOT before a

          large load customer may be interconnected.

    (8)   Intermediate agreement -- An agreement that is executed by a large load

          customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different from the interconnecting DSP,

          the interconnecting TSP before the interconnection study are initiated and that, at a

    (9)   Large load customer -- An entity requesting a new or expanded interconnection

          where the customer’s total expected non-coincident peak demand at a single site is

          equal to or exceeds 75 MW.

    (6)   Backup generating facilities. A large load customer must disclose to the

  •   The Commission should not adopt a policy of directly assigning the cost of system

      with its existing business practices.

  •   Large loads with agreements signed ahead of the 2026 Regional Transmission Plan date

      (April 1, 2026) should not be subject to 16 TAC § 25.194(d) or 16 TAC § 25.194(f).

  •   In terms of agreements between a large load customer, an interconnecting Distribution

      Service Provider (DSP), and an interconnecting Transmission Service Provider (TSP), it is

      important to recognize that the TSP bears a disproportionate share of financial and

      regulatory risk and should therefore define the structure of the agreement. If the

      Commission moves towards creating a standard form, the TSP must retain the study fee

      defined    in    16    TAC § 25.194(d)(9)        and   financial    security    defined    in

      16 TAC § 25.194(d)(10).
